sections.skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices

questions.prompt: Kai has $200. He can buy a game console accessory or save toward a used bike. If he buys the accessory, what is the opportunity cost?

choices.text: The $200 price of the accessory itself, paid at the register
Nothing, because he still has the accessory
The sales tax on the accessory
The progress toward the bike that he gives up

questions.correct_answer: The progress toward the bike that he gives up
questions.intro: Every spending choice has an opportunity cost: the next-best thing you give up. Thinking about what else money could do helps you choose deliberately rather than automatically.
questions.feedback: Choosing the accessory means giving up progress toward the bike, the next-best option.

misconceptions.A: Confuses price with what is given up

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A sign says "Was $200, now $120!" Mia feels the $120 price is a great deal, even though similar items cost $100 elsewhere. Which bias is at work?

choices.text: Sunk cost thinking about money already spent
Loss aversion about a past investment loss
The bandwagon effect from friends' choices
Anchoring on the "was" price

questions.intro: Anchoring is relying too much on the first number you see. A high "original" price can make a sale price feel cheap, even when it is not a good deal compared with other options.
questions.feedback: The $200 anchor makes $120 seem cheap; comparing with $100 elsewhere shows it is not.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Leo paid $60 for a concert ticket but feels sick on the day. He goes anyway "so the money isn't wasted." What is this called?

choices.text: The sunk cost fallacy
Opportunity cost bias
Anchoring
Comparison shopping

questions.intro: A sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered. The sunk cost fallacy is letting it drive a new decision. Good decisions compare the future benefits and costs of each option.
questions.feedback: The $60 is gone either way; the choice should depend on how he feels and what he gains now.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Ana often buys things online late at night and regrets them. Which strategy targets this habit directly?

choices.text: Save her card details on every site so checkout is faster
Turn on more shopping notifications
Shop only during sales events
Wait 24 hours before buying anything not planned

questions.correct_answer: Wait 24 hours before buying anything not planned
questions.intro: Present bias is valuing what we want now much more than what we want later. Impulse buying feeds on it. Adding a delay, such as a 24-hour rule or removing saved cards, gives the planning part of the brain time to weigh in.
questions.feedback: A waiting period interrupts impulse buying and lets her compare the purchase with her goals.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which ordering follows a sound decision process?

choices.text: Set a goal, list options, compare, choose, review
Choose quickly, then find reasons to justify the choice later
List options, choose the most popular, skip review
Compare costs only after buying

questions.correct_answer: Set a goal, list options, compare, choose, review
questions.feedback: A deliberate process defines the goal and compares options before choosing, then reviews the result.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
sections.relationship: Recognizing biases requires first knowing what a reasoned choice looks like.

questions.prompt: Sam is choosing a phone plan. What are "alternatives"?

choices.text: The different plans he could choose
The reasons he wants a new phone now
The phone he already owns
The bill he paid last month

questions.correct_answer: The different plans he could choose
questions.intro: Every decision has alternatives (the options) and criteria (what matters to you, such as price, quality, or coverage). Good choices compare alternatives using your criteria.
questions.feedback: Alternatives are the options he is choosing among.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Sam wants the phone plan with the lowest ongoing cost. Which criterion fits that goal?

choices.text: A free phone case that comes with the plan
How many friends use the same carrier
Which carrier has the most TV ads
Monthly price

questions.intro: A criterion (plural: criteria) is a standard you use to judge options. Which criteria matter depends on your goal, such as ongoing cost, data, or coverage.
questions.feedback: For lowest ongoing cost, the monthly price is the criterion that matters.

misconceptions.A: A one-time perk, not an ongoing cost

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Plan A: $35, 5 GB. Plan B: $45, unlimited. Sam uses about 3 GB a month. Which plan fits his criteria of low cost and enough data?

choices.text: Plan A
Plan B, because unlimited always sounds better
Neither, because both cost money
Plan B, because it costs more

questions.feedback: Plan A covers his 3 GB for $10 less per month.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Plan A costs $35 a month and Plan B costs $45 a month. What is the yearly savings from choosing Plan A?
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: After choosing, why review the decision a month later?

choices.text: Because contracts require monthly reviews
To find someone to blame
Because reviewing a purchase lowers its price later
To check whether the choice worked as expected

questions.correct_answer: To check whether the choice worked as expected
questions.feedback: Reviewing lets you learn and adjust future choices.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A website shows "Only 2 left!" and a countdown timer. What is the intended effect?

choices.text: Rushing the buyer before comparing options
Helping the buyer compare options calmly
Lowering the price
Showing the store's full inventory honestly

questions.correct_answer: Rushing the buyer before comparing options
questions.intro: Scarcity and urgency messages ("only a few left," countdown timers) push quick decisions. Sometimes they are true, sometimes not. Slowing down protects your budget.
questions.feedback: Urgency cues are designed to cut comparison short.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A "free trial" requires a card and converts to $14.99 a month unless cancelled. What should Nia do before signing up?

choices.text: Assume it will cancel itself automatically
Use a friend's card instead
Ignore the terms, since the trial is advertised as free
Set a reminder to cancel before the trial ends

questions.correct_answer: Set a reminder to cancel before the trial ends
questions.feedback: Free trials often become paid subscriptions automatically; a reminder prevents unwanted charges.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A store's loyalty program gives 5% back in points. Raj spends $200 more than he planned to earn points. What did he gain compared with not overspending?

choices.text: He saved $10
He broke even
He saved $200
He spent $190 more, net of $10 in points

questions.correct_answer: He spent $190 more, net of $10 in points
questions.feedback: 5% of $200 = $10 in points, but he spent $200 extra: a net cost of $190.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which design choice is a "dark pattern" that makes spending easier than intended?

choices.text: Showing the total price before checkout
Listing all fees clearly up front
Making cancellation much harder than signing up
Offering a clear "cancel" button on every account page

questions.correct_answer: Making cancellation much harder than signing up
questions.intro: "Dark patterns" are design tricks that steer people into choices they did not intend, such as hidden fees, pre-checked add-ons, or hard-to-find cancellation steps.
questions.feedback: Easy sign-up and hard cancellation is a common dark pattern.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: At checkout, a $4.99 "protection plan" box is already checked on Ben's $25 order. What should he do?

choices.text: Uncheck it unless he decided he wants it
Leave it, since stores must check what customers need
Pay it, because it is under $5
Buy two to be safe

questions.correct_answer: Uncheck it unless he decided he wants it
questions.feedback: Pre-checked add-ons rely on default bias; $4.99 is about 20% of a $25 order.

misconceptions.C: Ignores that it is 20% of the order

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: An influencer promotes a product with a discount code. Which fact matters MOST?

choices.text: The influencer may be paid for each sale
The influencer has many followers
The video looks professional and well produced
The product is popular this week

questions.correct_answer: The influencer may be paid for each sale
questions.intro: Influencers are often paid to promote products and may earn money from each sale. Federal rules require disclosure of these relationships, but the incentive still shapes the message.
questions.feedback: A paid relationship is a reason to compare reviews and prices independently.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Friends spend $80 on a dinner out each weekend. Tara's budget allows $30. Which choice best balances friendship and her budget?

choices.text: Join every time and put the extra on a credit card
Skip all social events forever
Join for a lower-cost part or suggest a cheaper place
Cut her rent payment to afford it

questions.correct_answer: Join for a lower-cost part or suggest a cheaper place
questions.feedback: Adapting the plan keeps both the friendships and the budget.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Seeing friends' purchases online makes Eli feel he must buy similar things. What is this effect sometimes called?

choices.text: Compound interest
Diversification
Amortization
Social comparison, or "keeping up with the Joneses"

questions.correct_answer: Social comparison, or "keeping up with the Joneses"
questions.feedback: Comparing ourselves with others can push spending beyond our plans.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which statement about money and values is MOST accurate?

choices.text: More spending always leads to more happiness over time
Values have no effect on financial choices
Spending that matches your priorities satisfies more
Everyone should have the same priorities

questions.correct_answer: Spending that matches your priorities satisfies more
questions.feedback: Aligning spending with personal priorities, not others' expectations, improves satisfaction.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Tara writes her top three money priorities and checks big purchases against them. What does this help with?

choices.text: Raising her credit limit so priorities are easier to afford
Avoiding all spending
Spending first and checking priorities later
Making choices that match her goals

questions.correct_answer: Making choices that match her goals
questions.feedback: Written priorities act as criteria for decisions.

misconceptions.A: Thinks more credit makes goals easier

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.
